lead: Chaincode is the smart contract of Hyperledger Fabric. It is a program, written in Go, Java or Node.js, that runs in a container on a peer and reads or writes channel state through a shim API. Only a few universities teach its lifecycle in detail. Banks and consortia use chaincode for transfers, trade documents and claims where each organisation must endorse a change before the ledger accepts it.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for peers, orderers and channels, and Unit 5 for the general smart-contract idea.

blocks.text: Chaincode is application logic that owns a namespace on a channel. A namespace is a key prefix such as car; a key CAR1 becomes carCAR1, so two chaincodes do not collide.

Every chaincode runs inside a container started by the peer. The container talks to the peer through the shim API: GetState, PutState, DelState and GetStateByRange. A read-write set is the list of keys read and values to write. The API is the only door to the ledger.

Execution must be deterministic. The same proposal on two endorsing peers must produce the same read-write set, so code must not use random numbers, wall-clock time, external HTTP calls or local files. Pass such data as arguments.

Solidity contracts run on every Ethereum node under the EVM and pay gas. Fabric chaincode runs only on endorsing peers chosen by policy, uses permissioned identities, and has no gas; the cost is that the endorsement policy fixes who must run it. See Unit 5 for Solidity.

items: Install it on each endorsing peer.
Approve the definition for each organisation.
Commit the definition to the channel.
Invoke sends a transaction proposal; query calls a read-only function.

blocks.text: An endorsement policy names the organisations or peers that must sign the simulated result. A policy AND(OrgA.peer, OrgB.peer) needs both. A proposal goes to those peers; each runs the chaincode against its local state and returns a read-write set plus signature. The client sends the set to the orderer. The orderer cuts a block. Each committing peer checks the signatures, the policy and that the read-set versions are unchanged, then writes the write-set. If another transaction changed a key first, the read-set check fails and the transaction is invalid; it stays on the ledger but is not applied.
A private data collection keeps the value with authorised peers and puts only a hash on the shared ledger; other organisations see the hash, not the value.
A write to carCAR1 does not touch loanCAR1, because the namespace prefix is part of the key.

figure.caption: Both peers endorse (e = 2), which meets the AND policy's r = 2, so the block is committed and the owner becomes Ravi. With only Org A endorsing (e = 1 < r = 2), commit rejects the transaction and the owner stays Asha.

examples.question: CAR1 has owner Asha and price ₹5,00,000. TransferAsset(CAR1, Ravi) needs endorsements from Org A and Org B. Both peers endorse; the orderer includes the transaction in a block. State the owner after commit and after QueryAsset(CAR1). What if only Org A endorses?
steps: The policy is AND(OrgA.peer, OrgB.peer), so required endorsements r = 2.
The client sends the proposal to one peer in Org A and one in Org B.
Both peers simulate and return signed read-write sets; received endorsements e = 2.
e = 2 ≥ r = 2, so the client submits the endorsed set to the orderer.
The orderer puts the transaction in a block and sends the block to committing peers.
Commit validation passes; the write sets owner = Ravi in namespace carCAR1.
QueryAsset(CAR1) returns Ravi. With only Org A, e = 1 < r = 2, so commit rejects it and owner stays Asha.
examples.answer: The transfer commits and QueryAsset(CAR1) returns Ravi; with only Org A, 1 of 2 endorsements, the transaction is invalid and owner stays Asha.

traps: Execution changes the ledger immediately: it does not; only ordering and commit apply the write-set.
Endorsement is ordering or consensus: endorsement is simulation plus signature; the orderer only orders.
A query needs a block: queries read committed state and skip ordering.
AND and OR policies are read carelessly: AND needs every named peer, OR needs at least one.
Solidity gas and EVM rules apply to chaincode: they do not; Fabric has no gas in this sense.

quiz.q: What is chaincode and where does it run?
quiz.a: A Fabric smart contract program in a container on a peer; it uses the shim API to read and write channel state.

quiz.q: Why must chaincode execution be deterministic?
quiz.a: Endorsing peers must return the same read-write set; random numbers, time or network calls can make the sets differ.

quiz.q: Policy is AND(OrgA.peer, OrgB.peer). Org A endorses, Org B does not. Is the transaction valid at commit?
quiz.a: No. Required endorsements r = 2, received e = 1, so e < r and the commit check rejects it.

quiz.q: TransferAsset commits owner Ravi. A query runs before the commit block is written. What owner does it see?
quiz.a: Asha. A query reads committed state; the change exists only after commit.

quiz.q: Why does Fabric validate the read-set at commit?
quiz.a: Two transactions may read the same old value and write conflicting values; the version check rejects the later one to prevent lost updates.

quiz.q: Give two differences between Fabric chaincode and a Solidity contract.
quiz.a: Chaincode runs on policy-selected endorsing peers, not every node; it uses permissioned identities and no gas, while Solidity runs on the EVM and pays gas.

quiz.q: What is stored on the shared ledger for a private data collection?
quiz.a: Only a hash of the private value; authorised peers keep the value in their private database.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry Fabric networks deploy chaincode with lifecycle approvals, use private data collections for prices, and expose chaincode through the Fabric Gateway. Newer curricula add chaincode-as-a-service and token SDKs. Search for Fabric asset-transfer chaincode, private data collections, and Fabric Gateway.
